content: Frequency probability is an interpretation of probability that defines the likelihood of an event as the limit of its relative frequency in a large number of trials. This approach, known as the frequentist interpretation, addresses some of the issues associated with the previously dominant classical interpretation of probability. Frequentist statistics is closely associated with the work of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson, who developed the logical framework for statistical hypothesis testing. Other notable contributors to the frequentist school include John Venn and Richard von Mises. Frequentists discuss probabilities only in the context of well-defined random experiments. The set of all possible outcomes of such an experiment is referred to as the sample space. An event is defined as a specific subset of the sample space that is of interest. For any given event, only one of two outcomes is possible: the event either occurs or does not occur. The relative frequency of an event's occurrence, observed over multiple repetitions of the experiment, serves as a measure of the event's probability. Mathematically, if ( n_t ) represents the total number of trials and ( n_x ) represents the number of trials in which event ( x ) occurred, the probability ( P(x) ) of the event occurring can be approximated by its relative frequency. A more contentious claim within this framework is that, in the long run, as the number of trials approaches infinity, the relative frequency will converge exactly to the true probability of the event. However, one criticism of this claim is that we can only ever observe a finite sequence of trials, making the extrapolation to an infinite number of trials a metaphysical assumption. This critique challenges the frequentist assertion that their interpretation is inherently more objective than other probability theories. The frequentist interpretation is a highly technical and scientific definition of probability. It does not aim to encompass all the connotations of the term probable as used in everyday language. This is analogous to how physicists use the concept of force in a precise manner, even though the term also appears in religious or philosophical contexts. In practice, the context usually clarifies whether the scientific or colloquial meaning is intended. The idea that the probable is that which for the most part happens was explicitly articulated by Robert Leslie Ellis in his 1842 work On the Foundations of the Theory of Probabilities and later in Remarks on the Fundamental Principles of the Theory of Probabilities. Antoine Augustin Cournot presented a similar conception in 1843 in his Exposition de la théorie des chances et des probabilités. Perhaps the first comprehensive and systematic exposition of this idea was provided by John Venn in his work The Logic of Chance: An Essay on the Foundations and Province of the Theory of Probability, published in 1866 and revised in subsequent editions. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the term frequentist was first used by M.G. Kendall in 1949 to distinguish this school of thought from the Bayesian approach, which he referred to as non-frequentist (citing Harold Jeffreys).
